body: Kneeling in his own hallway on a Saturday in October, a man is cutting floorboards. The water came in one night in January, stood at about the height of a kitchen chair, and was in the house two days before it went anywhere. He has done the skirting. The new boards are oak, like the old ones, and they are not the same colour as the old ones, and in the front room where the water never reached the original floor is still down. He knows the join will be visible from the front door for as long as he owns the house. He lays them anyway. He puts the kettle on at eleven and again at three.

That is what restoration looks like when you can stand in a doorway and watch it happen. The house works again. The house is not the house it was in December, and no further work will make it that house.

Restoration language gets used loosely in church, and the looseness sets people up badly. What a listener takes away is that the thing lost will be handed back in its original condition, and when it is not, the promise looks broken rather than misheard.

So look at what is actually promised. Joel says the years the locusts ate will be restored to you. Read that slowly, because it is more precise than it sounds. The years are restored — not the locusts undone, not that summer’s harvest reissued, not the season lifted off the calendar as though nothing had eaten it. Job ends the book with more than he began with, and the sons and daughters at the end are not the sons and daughters who died in it, and the book never pretends they are. The New Testament word translated restore keeps its ordinary sense of putting something back into working order — the same word used of fishermen mending their nets. Mended nets fish. They also have a mend in them, and everyone handling them knows exactly where.

This band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. One entire frequency is given over to nothing but the promises — declaration rather than mood, which is a harder format to sustain and a harder one to fill.

Preaching it precisely costs a room something on the day. The bigger promise is easier to say and people thank you for it on the way out. The smaller promise is the one still standing eleven years later when somebody checks it against what actually happened to them. That is the trade this band has taken, knowingly. Joel promises the years the locusts ate will be restored. It does not promise the locusts never came, and a station that implies otherwise is writing a cheque against somebody else’s account.

The looser version is everywhere now, and it is not only a church problem. Nearly everything a person owns has become replaceable, and the language that comes with replacement has quietly taught us what a loss is supposed to end like. Made whole. Like for like. As new. We have been trained to expect that a loss properly handled ends with an identical item in the same place, and we carry that to the handful of things that do not work that way at all — which are, without exception, the things that matter. Nobody decided to teach us this. It arrived with the paperwork.

So the covenant end of this dial is built around what is actually said rather than how it feels to hear it. The declaration records sing the promises back in the first person, one album for each of the twelve Inspire Family voices, and what is sung is not an atmosphere but a wording. A station arranged that way cannot inflate the offer, because it is not making it. It is repeating one, and a repetition can be checked against the original by anybody with a Bible and a free afternoon.
Which raises the obvious objection, and it is a fair one that deserves better than being brushed aside.

The objection is that the smaller promise is a colder one. Be fair to it: in the first month of a loss, precision sounds like a shortage of sympathy, and there are hours when a person needs somebody to say something enormous rather than something accurate. But look at what the enormous version does to that person over ten years. It arrives, they believe it, and the decade does not come back. So either God has failed or they have, and since they will not say the first out loud, they say the second quietly for years. A promise that cannot survive being read carefully is not a comfort. It is a debt, and it falls due on somebody.
Restoration is not a reversal. It is a rebuild.

It is a Wednesday evening in September and a woman of fifty-one is at an enrolment desk in a school hall, filling in a form for a course she should have done at nineteen. The queue behind her is mostly eighteen-year-olds standing with their mothers. She has to ask the man at the desk what to put in the box marked most recent qualification, and the true answer takes explaining, and he writes it down without comment. She pays the deposit in cash. In the car park she sits a minute before starting the engine, because she has not been inside a school since her own children left one. Then she drives home, puts the shopping away, and mentions it to nobody for a fortnight.

Nothing about that evening returned anything to her. She did not get the decade back. She got a Wednesday, a form and a receipt. That is what restoration looks like when it turns up, and it never announces itself as restoration at the time.

Here is what does not come back, said plainly, because half-saying it is worse. The years do not come back as years. The people do not come back. A marriage that ended is ended, a damaged body carries the damage, and a person who lost their twenties to an illness gets an ordinary set of forties rather than a second attempt at twenty-four. There are losses for which the only honest word in this life is loss. Anyone who says otherwise is selling something.

But that limit is not a hole in the promise; it is the shape of it, and the shape is why it can be trusted. A guarantee of erasure would require the past to become untrue, and a God who edits what happened can say nothing reliable about what is happening now — if January can be deleted, so can this morning. What is offered instead is a rebuild carried out by somebody who was present for the flood and did not leave during it. That is a smaller sentence and a far larger thing to be handed.

So capacity comes back. Function comes back. The ability to work, to trust somebody, to sit in a room full of people, to want the evening rather than merely survive it — those genuinely return, more slowly than anyone would like and often more completely than the person expected in the worst part of it. What does not come back is the timeline, and the promise never said it would. The join stays visible from the door. The house works.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming, and it is worth knowing they are there before you start turning. Music, which is most of the band — worship, hymns, gospel, country, ambient and a great deal besides. Teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. Family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards, 40 across 29 languages. Every station holds one frequency permanently, so a number found once can be returned to without looking.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 303.10 — Yes and Amen. It carries the declaration albums, one for each of the twelve Inspire Family voices, and what they sing is not how anybody feels that morning; it is what is already the case regardless. The name is a quotation, and it is the reason to send you here rather than anywhere else at the end of this article: every promise of God is Yes and Amen in Him. When you have stopped being certain what was actually promised — when the thing you were told would be given back has not been, and you cannot tell whether you misheard or were misled — the useful station is not the one that agrees with your mood. It is the one that keeps repeating the wording until you can hear where the wording ends.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people reach for and when — which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation and not an offer. Put HM 303.10 on while you are doing something ordinary — laying a floor, filling in a form, waiting for a kettle at three in the afternoon — and let it repeat itself at you for a fortnight. Do not wait until you feel restored before listening to a station about restoration. That was always the wrong order, and the man in the hallway did not wait for the floor to match before he started laying it.
